summaries.example: Imagine that a prince’s thoughts and memories somehow moved into a cobbler’s body. Locke asks us to consider whether the person would be the prince or the cobbler. His answer points toward consciousness: the person would go with the continuing awareness of the prince’s experiences, even though the body had changed.
summaries.summary: John Locke asked what makes someone the same person over time. He distinguished a person from a human body and from a soul. For Locke, a person is a thinking, self-aware being who can be responsible for actions. Personal identity depends on the continuation of consciousness: the awareness that connects a present self with earlier thoughts and actions. This means that the same human being might not always be the same person, in Locke’s unusual examples. He also says that a person could remain the same even if the body or soul changed, as long as consciousness continued. Philosophers have disagreed about what Locke meant by consciousness and whether he was describing reality itself or only what people can know about themselves. His ideas have influenced many later discussions of memory, minds, bodies, and selves.
key_ideas: Locke says we must first understand what we mean by “person” before asking what makes a person stay the same.
Personal identity depends on sameness of consciousness, not simply on having the same body or soul.
A human being, a soul, and a person are different ideas, even though they may belong together in ordinary life.
Locke uses unusual imagined stories to test what we think makes someone the same person.
summaries.why_it_matters: Locke’s view helps us ask careful questions about responsibility and change. We grow, forget, and change our bodies, but we still wonder what connects us to our past and future selves. His distinctions also show why ordinary words such as “human,” “soul,” and “person” may not answer the same question.

important_terms.definition: A person is a thinking being that can understand, reflect on itself, and be responsible for what it does.
Awareness of your own thoughts and experiences. Locke connects it with knowing yourself as the same self over time.
Being the very same individual at different times. Locke asks what makes a person remain the same.
A human being considered as a living animal. Locke says a human being and a person are not always exactly the same idea.
A word used when someone can be praised, blamed, rewarded, or punished for an action.

questions_to_think_about: If someone forgot an action completely, would that change who they are?
Is having the same body enough to make someone the same person?
Could you still be the same person after a big change in your thoughts?
Why might being responsible for an action matter when we talk about identity?

summaries.example: Consider Locke’s day-and-night case: one body is imagined to be guided by one stream of consciousness during the day and another at night. Locke suggests that these could count as two persons, even if they share one body and one soul. The example separates personal identity from bodily and spiritual sameness, while also linking personhood to accountability for actions.
summaries.summary: Locke’s central question is not simply whether a body or soul continues, but what makes a person the same person across time. He first argues that identity must be considered relative to a kind: the persistence of a mass of matter, plant, animal, human being, or person may have different conditions. A person is a rational and reflective agent capable of recognizing itself as itself and of being accountable under laws. Locke then identifies personal identity with sameness of consciousness. Consciousness can extend backward to earlier thoughts and actions, making those actions attributable to the present person. His thought experiments—a prince’s consciousness associated with a cobbler’s body, separated waking and sleeping consciousnesses, and day-and-night persons—are designed to pull apart person, human being, body, and soul. Locke therefore denies that the identity of a person simply consists in the identity of a substance. He remains cautious about whether finite thinkers are immaterial or material, arguing that our knowledge of underlying substance is limited and that thinking might, for all we know, be added to matter by God. Interpretations differ sharply: some read Locke as offering an epistemological account of how identity is judged, while others see metaphysical claims about what makes a person persist. Further debates concern whether consciousness is memory, a continuing center of awareness, or the appropriation of mental events as one’s own. Critics such as Butler and Reid raised problems about circularity and transitivity, but Locke’s framework continues to shape psychological-continuity theories and competing views such as animalism.
key_ideas: Locke begins with a place-time-kind principle: two things of the same kind cannot occupy one place at one time, and one individual cannot be in two places at once.
Because different kinds have different persistence conditions, identity cannot be settled by substance alone.
Sameness of person consists in sameness of consciousness extending backward to past thoughts and actions; this supports Locke’s account of responsibility.
Locke separates person, human being, body, and soul. A change in one does not automatically determine a change in the others.
Scholars debate whether Locke is making metaphysical claims about what persons are or epistemological claims about how we judge identity.
Later objections, including concerns about circularity and contradiction, and later psychological-continuity theories, show the continuing influence of Locke’s account.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate connects metaphysics with ethics. If personhood involves consciousness and accountability, then questions about memory, responsibility, future concern, and psychological change become central to identity. Locke also established a method of using imagined cases to expose assumptions about bodies, souls, and selves. Even philosophers who reject his conclusions often define their positions by responding to his distinctions.

important_terms.definition: The condition by which an individual remains numerically the same across different times; for Locke, the relevant condition differs by kind, such as body, animal, or person.
A thinking, reflective agent that can regard itself as itself across times and places and can be held accountable for actions.
The awareness accompanying thought and allowing a self to connect itself with earlier thoughts or actions.
A condition for remaining the same kind of thing over time. Locke argues that it must be determined after the kind itself is understood.
The underlying substance that supports qualities. Locke holds that finite minds cannot fully know what such an underlying substance is.
The view that identity questions must specify what kind of thing is being tracked, such as a body, human being, soul, or person.
A term concerning agency, law, reward, and punishment; it marks a person as accountable for actions.
The view that personal identity depends on continuing psychological life, such as consciousness, rather than merely bodily continuity.

questions_to_think_about: Does remembering an action make you the person who performed it, or does memory merely provide evidence of identity?
Can Locke’s account avoid a contradiction when consciousness links some past stages but not others?
Is a person best understood as a substance, a mode, a relation, or something else?
What would be gained or lost by treating personal identity as a matter of psychological continuity rather than bodily continuity?
How does accountability affect the philosophical meaning of “person”?

summaries.example: Suppose your classmate wakes up one morning with memories and thoughts that seem to belong to another student, while the body has not changed. Locke’s prince-and-cobbler idea asks us to decide which person is present. The example suggests that the person follows the continuing consciousness, not automatically the body. Locke does not claim this normally happens; he uses it to separate ideas we usually blend together.
summaries.summary: John Locke’s account of personal identity begins by separating several ideas that people often treat as one: human being, body, soul, and person. He says that each kind of thing may have its own way of remaining the same over time. A person is a thinking, reflective agent who can recognize itself across different times and can be held accountable for what it does. Locke’s key proposal is that personal identity depends on sameness of consciousness. If present consciousness reaches back to a past thought or action, then the present person is connected with the person who had that experience. His examples of a prince and a cobbler, of waking and sleeping versions of Socrates, and of separate day and night consciousnesses are meant to show that personal identity can come apart from bodily or spiritual identity. Locke also questions whether we can know the underlying substance of a thinking being. He does not firmly settle whether finite thinkers are made of immaterial substance or whether matter could be given the power to think. Later readers have debated whether consciousness is simply memory, a continuing center of awareness, or a person’s taking certain experiences as their own. Critics argued that Locke’s view may be circular or may create problems when memories connect some stages of a life but not others. Even so, his account became a major starting point for later theories that explain identity through mental or psychological continuity.
key_ideas: Locke says we need to define a kind of thing before deciding what makes it remain the same.
For persons, the important link is continuing consciousness, not just the same body, soul, or material parts.
A person is also an agent who can be responsible for actions and receive reward or punishment.
Locke’s imagined cases challenge the assumption that one human being, one body, one soul, and one person must always be identical.
Philosophers disagree about whether Locke explains real identity or only how people can know and judge identity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Locke’s ideas matter because they connect the question “Who am I?” with memory, responsibility, and change. They also teach an important philosophical lesson: a single word such as “same” can hide different questions. We might ask whether the same body, human being, soul, or person continues, and those questions may not have the same answer.

important_terms.definition: The question of what makes something remain the same individual as time passes.
Awareness of your thoughts and experiences, including the ability to connect yourself with your earlier self.
A thinking and self-aware being that can plan, reflect, and be held responsible for actions.
A human animal or human being. Locke treats this as a different category from “person,” even though they often overlap.
The idea that no two things of the same kind can be in the same place at the same time, and one thing cannot be in two places at once.
The underlying stuff or support beneath an object’s qualities. Locke says we have very limited knowledge of it.
A relation between present and past mental life that helps explain why later philosophers connect Locke with psychological continuity.

questions_to_think_about: Would a person remain the same after losing some memories?
Can two persons share one body in Locke’s imagined cases?
Why might Locke distinguish a human being from a person?
Is consciousness the same thing as memory, or could it be broader?
Which seems more important for identity: the body, the mind, or responsibility?
